blocks.text: A class captain in Abeokuta puts twenty identical slips in a bowl — five of them have Lagos written on the back — and picks one without looking. How likely is it that the slip says Lagos? Probability turns that everyday chance into a number between 0 and 1 that you can calculate, estimate and compare.

blocks.markdown:
An **experiment** is a repeatable action with more than one possible result (tossing a coin, throwing a die, picking a student). A single result is an **outcome**. The **sample space** $S$ is the set of all possible outcomes.

For a fair coin tossed twice, $S = \{HH, HT, TH, TT\}$. For two fair dice thrown together, $S$ has $6 \times 6 = 36$ ordered pairs.

When every outcome in $S$ is equally likely,

$P(A) = \frac{\text{number of outcomes in } A}{\text{number of outcomes in } S}$.

Always $0 \le P(A) \le 1$. An impossible event has probability $0$; a certain event has probability $1$.

blocks.title: The complement rule
blocks.text: The complement $A'$ is the event that $A$ does not happen. Because $A$ and $A'$ together cover the whole sample space and do not overlap, $P(A') = 1 - P(A)$. Use this whenever "not" is easier than listing what you want.

blocks.caption: Theoretical probability when outcomes are equally likely

blocks.title: Complement of "green"
blocks.prompt: A bag contains 3 red, 5 blue and 2 green balls. One ball is drawn at random. Find the probability that it is not green.

blocks.markdown:
### Experimental (relative-frequency) probability

When the outcomes are not known to be equally likely, or when you are given trial data, estimate the probability from the experiment:

$P(A) \approx \frac{\text{number of times } A \text{ occurred}}{\text{number of trials}}$.

A die thrown $80$ times that shows a $4$ on $12$ of them gives the estimate $\frac{12}{80} = \frac{3}{20}$, not the theoretical $\frac{1}{6}$. In a long run of trials the experimental value usually moves towards the theoretical one, but a single exam question wants the estimate from the numbers you are given.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Write probabilities as a fraction in lowest terms, a decimal, or a percentage — never as a ratio such as $1:5$, and never as a number greater than $1$. If a question gives experimental counts, do not replace them with the theoretical fair-die or fair-coin value.

points: The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes of an experiment.
For equally likely outcomes, $P(A)$ is favourable outcomes divided by the size of $S$.
Experimental probability is frequency of the event divided by the number of trials.
List $HT$ and $TH$ as different outcomes when order matters.
